text: Your marketing team sends a redesigned email to 40 customers and the old email to another 40. The new email's customers spent an average of $58.20 per order; the old email's customers spent $52.57. Is the new email better, or did you just get a lucky batch of shoppers? Hypothesis testing is the formal, repeatable way to answer that — and every test in the rest of this chapter is a variation on the same idea.

Two groups of customers will never have exactly the same average, even if the email makes no difference at all. Random variation between people alone guarantees a gap. The real question is: is this gap bigger than the gaps that chance produces by itself? Standard error from Lesson 17 described how much sample statistics wobble — hypothesis testing turns that idea into an actual decision.

A hypothesis test sets two competing claims. The null hypothesis says nothing interesting is going on — the two emails produce the same average order value, any gap is chance. The alternative says there's a real difference. We test the null because it's precise — no difference gives us one concrete world to simulate, while some difference could mean a dollar or a hundred dollars, and you can't simulate a vague claim.

The logic mirrors a courtroom. The defendant is presumed innocent, the null, until the evidence is unlikely enough under that presumption that we reject it. Failing to convict doesn't prove innocence, and failing to reject the null doesn't prove no effect — it only says the evidence wasn't strong enough.

The four-step recipe: state H0 and H1 before you look at the results, pick a test statistic that measures the gap, ask how often chance alone would produce a statistic at least this extreme if H0 were true, and if that probability is small enough, reject H0. Classical tests like the t-test use a formula for step three; a permutation test uses brute force, and it makes the logic visible.

If the email truly made no difference, the labels old and new are meaningless, so we can shuffle them freely and see what gaps arise by luck alone. Simulated data: the new email's customers average 58 dollars, old averages 52, an observed gap of 5.62. Now pool all 80 orders, shuffle, split into fake groups of 40, and record the gap — repeated 10,000 times.

In this run, only about 3.4 percent of the shuffles produced a gap as large as 5.62 in either direction. That number is the p-value, the subject of the next lesson. It says: in a world where the email does nothing, a gap this big would be rare, so the null looks hard to defend.

A small probability lets you reject H0 — the data are hard to explain by chance alone. It does not tell you the size of the effect, that it matters commercially, or that the email caused it, which depends on how the groups were formed, a theme returning in Chapter 6. And a large probability means inconclusive, not proven identical.

To recap: hypothesis testing compares your observed statistic to what chance alone would produce under the null. You state H0 and H1, choose a test statistic, work out how surprising your result would be if H0 were true, and decide. A permutation test does this by shuffling; formula-based tests do it with math. Next, we look closely at the number that comes out: the p-value.
